notes: Slot 7 = neo-Ba'athist Regional Command (Atassi/Jadid). Assad's military wing is carried by slot 22 (armed forces). Arab Socialist Movement moved from MD slot 5 to slot 3 (has starting popularity). Pro-Iraqi Ba'ath kept in slot 21 per MD; SSNP slot 20 per MD. Slot 6 = Habannaka's Maydan ulama (hardline anti-secular, anti-Western conservatives).

0.name: Al-Infisaliyyun
0.text:
The Secessionists are the officers and politicians of the 1961 coup that broke Syria away from the United Arab Republic and ran the country until the Ba'athist takeover of March 1963. Purged, imprisoned or driven abroad, they now live in Beirut, Amman and Riyadh. Colonel Abd al-Karim al-Nahlawi, who led the 1961 putsch, and former prime minister Ma'mun al-Kuzbari are their best-known names.

The Secessionists want a strong-armed restoration of private property, the old parliament and close ties with Saudi Arabia, Jordan and the West. Their base is the dispossessed landowning and merchant class and a few cashiered Sunni officers. Their leverage depends entirely on foreign patrons and on a split inside the Syrian army.

1.name: Hizb al-Sha'b
1.text:
The People's Party was founded in 1948 by Aleppo notables who resented the Damascene leadership of the independence movement. It dominated parliament in the 1950s and returned briefly to power after the 1961 secession, when Nazim al-Kudsi became president. The Ba'ath dissolved it in 1963, and its leaders, among them Rushdi al-Kikhya, now live in silence or exile.

The party stands for constitutional government, private enterprise and closer ties with Iraq and the Hashemite world. It is wary of Cairo and hostile to the Soviet orientation of the regime. Its base lies among the merchants, landowners and urban notables of Aleppo and Homs, whose wealth and family networks survive the nationalizations.

2.name: Al-Hizb al-Watani
2.text:
The National Party grew out of the National Bloc that led Syria to independence from France. Shukri al-Quwatli, its towering figure, died in Beirut in 1967. Sabri al-Asali, three times prime minister in the 1950s, is the most prominent surviving leader. The Ba'athist regime banned the party in 1963, and its old notables live on the margins of public life.

The party is liberal-constitutionalist in temperament. It favours parliamentary government, a free press, private trade and a neutral, Arab nationalist foreign policy tilted towards Egypt and Saudi Arabia rather than either superpower. Its strength lies in the great Damascene families and in the memory of the independence era.

3.name: Harakat al-Ishtirakiyyin al-Arab
3.text:
The Arab Socialist Movement is the party of Akram al-Hawrani, the Hama tribune who roused the peasants of central Syria against the landlords in the 1940s. He merged it into the Ba'ath in 1952, broke away again after supporting the 1961 secession, and refounded it as his own movement. Since 1963 Hawrani has lived in exile and his followers are kept out of power.

The movement wants land reform, parliamentary democracy and social justice without a one-party state. It is hostile to both the military Ba'ath and the old notables, and keeps its distance from Moscow. Its base is the peasantry and lower middle class of Hama and the Orontes valley, where Hawrani's name still carries weight.

4.name: Al-Hizb al-Shuyu'i al-Suri
4.text:
The Syrian Communist Party is the oldest communist party in the Arab world, and Khalid Bakdash has led it for more than three decades. It is still formally illegal, but since 1966 the neo-Ba'athist regime has tolerated it, allowed Bakdash to return from exile and given a communist, Samih Atiyah, a seat in the cabinet.

The party follows Moscow's line closely. It backs the alliance with the Soviet Union, nationalization and land reform while pressing for a legal front with the Ba'ath. Its members are Kurds in Damascus, Christian and Alawite intellectuals, teachers and trade unionists. Its leverage comes from Soviet patronage, which the regime cannot afford to ignore.

5.name: Al-Sa'iqa
5.native_full: Tala'i' Harb al-Tahrir al-Sha'biyya – Quwwat al-Sa'iqa
5.text:
As-Sa'iqa, the Vanguards of the Popular War of Liberation, is the Palestinian guerrilla organization the Syrian Ba'ath created in 1966. Salah Jadid's party apparatus finances, arms and directs it. After the 1967 defeat it grew into one of the largest fedayeen forces in the Palestine Liberation Organization, with bases in Syria, Jordan and southern Lebanon.

Sa'iqa preaches people's war against Israel and revolution against the Arab monarchies, and it serves as the armed arm of the regime's radical wing. Its fighters come from the Palestinian refugee camps and from young Ba'athist volunteers. Its leverage lies in its weapons and its place in the PLO, and in Jadid's readiness to use it against rivals at home and abroad.

6.name: Ulama al-Maydan
6.text:
The Ulama of the Maydan are the scholars, preachers and merchants gathered around Shaykh Hasan Habannaka al-Maydani in the old Maydan quarter of Damascus. Habannaka led the mosque strikes of 1964 and the protests of 1967 against an army journal article attacking religion, and spent time in prison for it. On 1 January 1970 the circle is watched closely but cannot be silenced.

The ulama reject secularism, socialism and the regime's Soviet friendship, but they distrust the West just as deeply. They demand that Islam be the religion of the state, that religious schools be protected and that the suq be left alone. Their base is the conservative Sunni lower middle class of Damascus, and their leverage is the Friday sermon.

7.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki – Qutr Suriya
7.english: Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party – Syria Region
7.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki – Qutr Suriya
7.text:
The Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party has ruled Syria since March 1963. The coup of 23 February 1966 drove out the party founders Michel Aflaq and Salah al-Din al-Bitar and brought the radical neo-Ba'athists to power. Nureddin al-Atassi is head of state and prime minister, but the real power behind the party apparatus is Salah Jadid, the assistant regional secretary.

The neo-Ba'ath preaches scientific socialism, nationalization, land reform and people's war against Israel, and it relies on the Soviet Union for weapons and aid. Its cadres are rural Alawite, Druze, Ismaili and Sunni officers and teachers. Its weakness is the army: Defence Minister Hafez al-Assad has built his own power base there.
7.wiki: Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party – Syria Region

8.name: Al-Madrasa al-Muhsiniyya
8.text:
The Muhsiniyya School in the Amara quarter of Damascus is the intellectual home of the city's small Twelver Shia community. Sayyid Muhsin al-Amin, the reforming cleric from Jabal Amil who led the Damascene Shia until his death in 1952, founded it. His family and students still keep its schools and charities running under the Ba'athist regime.

The Muhsiniyya tradition stands for modern education, the reform of popular rituals and cooperation with Arab nationalism. It wants civil equality for the Shia rather than clerical rule. Its base is the Shia families of old Damascus and their links to Lebanon's Jabal Amil. Its leverage is its scholarly prestige and its ties to the Lebanese Shia awakening.

9.name: Mujawiru al-Sayyida Zaynab
9.text:
The Neighbours of Sayyida Zaynab are the Iraqi, Iranian and Lebanese clerics and seminarians who have settled around the shrine of Sayyida Zaynab south of Damascus. Their numbers grow as the Iraqi Ba'ath persecutes the seminaries of Najaf and Karbala, and their small study circles at the shrine are becoming a meeting point for militant Shia exiles.

The circle wants the faithful to follow the leading jurists in all public affairs. It rejects secular nationalism, the Shah's monarchy and the Ba'ath parties of Baghdad and Damascus alike. Its base is the shrine community and the pilgrims who pass through. Its leverage lies in its ties to the seminaries of Najaf and Qom and to Shia networks across the region.

10.name: Dar al-Ifta
10.english: Office of the Grand Mufti of Syria
10.native_full: Dar al-Ifta fi al-Jumhuriyya al-Arabiyya al-Suriyya
10.text:
The Office of the Grand Mufti is the official religious authority of Sunni Islam in Syria. Since 1964 it has been headed by Shaykh Ahmad Kuftaro, the Naqshbandi Sufi master of the Abu al-Nur mosque in the Kurdish quarter of Damascus. He has chosen accommodation with the Ba'athist state in exchange for room to teach and preach.

The establishment ulama preach obedience to authority, moderation and spiritual renewal through mosques and Sufi orders, not political confrontation. They condemn the Muslim Brotherhood's militancy and give the regime religious cover. Their base is the mosque network, the ministry of religious endowments and Kuftaro's devoted followers. Their leverage is their role as the state's sanctioned voice of Islam.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party, was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani. He now directs it in secret from Beirut. It is banned in Syria, and its small, disciplined cells among students and junior officers are hunted by the security services, who suspect them of seeking a sympathetic army faction for a coup.

The party rejects every existing Arab state, nationalism and parliamentary politics, and aims to restore the caliphate in one stroke by winning over those who hold military power. It is equally hostile to American capitalism and Soviet communism. Its members are educated, urban and secretive. Its leverage is ideological, but it reaches across the whole Arab East.

12.name: Al-Ikhwan al-Muslimun fi Suriya
12.text:
The Syrian Muslim Brotherhood was founded in the 1940s by Mustafa al-Siba'i and sat in parliament in the 1950s. It has been banned since the Ba'athist takeover. Its general guide, Isam al-Attar, leads from exile in West Germany, while northern leaders such as Abd al-Fattah Abu Ghudda of Aleppo challenge his authority. In Hama, Marwan Hadid preaches armed struggle.

The Brotherhood demands an Islamic constitution, free elections and an end to minority rule by the Ba'athist officers. It is fiercely anti-communist and deeply suspicious of Soviet influence. Its strength lies in the Sunni towns of Hama, Aleppo, Homs and Damascus, among merchants, craftsmen, teachers and students who resent the regime.

13.name: Al-Ittihad al-Ishtiraki al-Arabi
13.text:
The Arab Socialist Union is the main Nasserist party in Syria. It was founded in 1964 by former Ba'athists and unionists who wanted to restore the union with Egypt. Its secretary-general is Jamal al-Atassi, a physician and former Ba'athist minister. It is barred from power but keeps a following and close contacts with Cairo.

The ASU calls for Arab unity under Gamal Abdel Nasser's leadership, state-led development and a single mass organization above parties. It rejects the sectarian army cliques of the Ba'ath. Its base is the Sunni urban middle class, teachers and officers who remember the United Arab Republic. Its leverage is Nasser's prestige among ordinary Syrians.

14.name: Partiya Demokrat a Kurdî li Sûriyê
14.native_full: Partiya Demokrat a Kurdî li Sûriyê
14.text:
The Kurdish Democratic Party in Syria, founded in 1957, is the first Kurdish party in the country. It has been illegal since its leaders were arrested in 1960, and since 1965 it has been split. Abd al-Hamid Hajj Darwish leads its moderate right wing and Osman Sabri its radical left. Mustafa Barzani is trying to reunite the factions.

The party demands cultural and political rights for the Kurds, the return of citizenship to those stripped of it in the 1962 Hasaka census, and an end to the Arab Belt plan. Its base is the Kurdish villages of the Jazira and Kurd Dagh and the Kurdish quarters of Damascus. Its leverage lies in its ties to Barzani's movement in Iraq.

15.name: Ghurfat Tijarat Dimashq
15.text:
The Damascus Chamber of Commerce, founded in Ottoman times, speaks for the great Sunni merchant families of the capital's suqs. The nationalizations of 1965 and the radical socialism of the Jadid regime have stripped them of banks, factories and import houses. Their old commercial dynasties, led by veterans such as Badr al-Din al-Shallah, still dominate retail and wholesale trade.

The merchants want an end to confiscations, a return to private import and export, and a government that respects property and the suq. They fund mosques and charities and keep quiet ties with Beirut's banks and the Gulf. Their leverage is economic: the strikes they closed the suqs with in 1964 and 1965 are remembered by every Ba'athist.

16.name: Ghurfat Sina'at Halab
16.text:
The Aleppo Chamber of Industry represents the textile and manufacturing families who built modern Syrian industry in the 1940s and 1950s. Most of their mills and companies were nationalized in 1965, and many owners have moved their capital and their sons to Beirut. Those who remain manage small workshops under suspicious official eyes.

Aleppo's industrialists believe in free enterprise, low tariffs on raw materials, open trade with Turkey, Lebanon and Iraq, and an end to state monopolies. They regard the planned economy as ruinous and Soviet advisers as an insult. Their base is the old Christian and Sunni bourgeoisie of Aleppo. Their leverage is their capital and expertise, which the state needs and cannot replace.

17.name: Hurras al-Ghuta
17.text:
The Guardians of the Ghouta are agronomists, engineers and orchard owners alarmed by what is happening to the green belt of gardens and orchards that has fed Damascus for millennia. The city's rapid growth, illegal building and the over-pumping of the Barada river are eating away at the Ghouta. Under Ba'athist rule they meet in agricultural societies and university faculties.

The Guardians call for protection of the Barada springs and the Ghouta orchards, reforestation of the coastal mountains and careful study of the Soviet-built Euphrates dam now under construction at Tabqa. They avoid open politics. Their base is the old garden villages around Damascus and the agricultural faculty. Their leverage is technical expertise the planners need.

18.name: Harakat al-Wahdawiyyin al-Ishtirakiyyin
18.text:
The Socialist Unionist Movement was founded in 1961 by Ba'athists who refused to accept the secession from the United Arab Republic and broke with the party leadership over it. Under Fayez Ismail it has become one of the main Nasserist-leaning socialist groups in Syria. It is tolerated but has no share in power.

The movement stands for Arab unity, socialism, land reform and a broad national front of progressive parties, and it backs a non-aligned foreign policy that still leans on Moscow for arms. Its base is teachers, civil servants, students and union activists in the cities. Its leverage lies in its Nasserist credentials and its readiness to join a front with the Ba'ath.

19.name: Hizb al-Ummal al-Thawri al-Arabi
19.text:
The Arab Revolutionary Workers Party was founded in the mid-1960s by Yasin al-Hafiz, a former Ba'athist theoretician. It gathers dissident Marxists who reject both the Ba'athist military state and the Soviet-line Syrian Communist Party. It is small, illegal and mainly a circle of intellectuals, writers and students in Damascus, Homs and Latakia.

The party blends Marxism with Arab nationalism, criticizes Stalinism and the bureaucratic socialism of the regime, and calls for genuine workers' democracy and a popular war of liberation. It looks with interest at China, Cuba and Vietnam rather than Moscow. Its influence lies in its ideas, which circulate widely among the Syrian and Lebanese left.

20.name: Al-Hizb al-Suri al-Qawmi al-Ijtima'i
20.text:
The Syrian Social Nationalist Party, founded in Beirut in 1932 by Antun Sa'adeh, was once a major force in Syrian politics. It was crushed after a member assassinated Colonel Adnan al-Malki in 1955 and has been banned in Syria ever since. Its leadership, including Abdallah Saadeh and In'am Ra'd, is based in Lebanon after the failed 1961 coup attempt there.

The party preaches the unity of Greater Syria from the Taurus to Sinai, secularism and a strong leader, and rejects both Arab nationalism and sectarian politics. It is anti-Zionist and anti-communist. Its supporters are Christians, Druze and secular minorities in Lebanon and western Syria. Its leverage is disciplined underground cells and armed veterans.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th – al-Qiyada al-Qawmiyya
21.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki – al-Qiyada al-Qawmiyya
21.text:
The National Command loyalists are the Syrian Ba'athists who stayed faithful to the party founder Michel Aflaq after the 1966 coup. Their leaders, including former president Amin al-Hafiz, fled to Beirut and later to Baghdad, where the Iraqi Ba'ath has adopted them since it took power in 1968. Inside Syria they are hunted as traitors.

The loyalists claim to be the true Ba'ath: Arab unity under one party, an authoritarian national state and the cult of the founding leadership. They denounce the Damascus regime as a sectarian military clique. Their base is exiled officers and Sunni party veterans. Their leverage depends on Iraqi money, Iraqi intelligence and any army officer willing to change sides.

22.name: Al-Quwwat al-Musallaha al-Arabiyya al-Suriyya
22.text:
The Syrian Arab Armed Forces have made and unmade governments since 1949. Since the 1967 defeat, Defence Minister Hafez al-Assad and Chief of Staff Mustafa Tlass have turned the army into a power base independent of Salah Jadid's party apparatus. In February 1969 Assad's tanks briefly occupied Damascus, and the two power centres now live in an uneasy truce.

Assad's officers want a pragmatic regime: rebuilt forces, Soviet weapons without ideological zeal, reconciliation with the Arab states, a ceasefire in the war of words with Egypt and Saudi Arabia, and an end to the adventurism of people's war. Their base is the officer corps, much of it Alawite and rural. Their leverage is control of the guns.

23.name: Ansar al-Bayt al-Hashimi
23.text:
The Partisans of the Hashemite House are the scattered notables who still remember the Arab Kingdom of Syria proclaimed under Faisal in 1920 and the Greater Syria plans of King Abdullah of Jordan. Many were once in the People's Party or tribal councils, and today they keep contact with the royal court in Amman.

The Partisans dream of a constitutional monarchy under the Hashemites, uniting Syria with Jordan and ending republican coups and military rule. They are pro-Western and staunchly anti-communist. Their base is a handful of old families in Aleppo, Hauran and the tribal east. Their leverage is negligible inside Syria and depends wholly on King Hussein's interest and Western support.
